description: The default identity LoginHandler maps ErrAccountLocked and ErrAccountDisabled to HTTP 429 "account_locked" while unknown identifiers and wrong passwords map to 401 "invalid_credentials" (identity/handlers.go mapAuthError, uniformAuthErrors=false by default). An unauthenticated attacker therefore learns account existence: (a) a disabled account answers 429 on the very first attempt vs 401 for unknown; (b) after N failed logins a real account flips to 429 while an unknown identifier stays 401 forever. This undercuts the service layer's decoy-hash anti-enumeration work at the HTTP boundary, and ships in the default webapp preset (webapp never sets WithUniformAuthErrors). PoC tests demonstrate both oracles end-to-end at the handler layer.
remediation: Fail closed by default: make uniform 401 "invalid_credentials" the default in newHandlerConfig (keep a distinct opt-in, e.g. WithVerboseLockoutStatus, for deployments that accept the oracle for UX), or set WithUniformAuthErrors() in the webapp preset. Concrete change: identity/handlers.go — default uniformAuthErrors=true; webapp/webapp.go — append identity.WithUniformAuthErrors() to idOpts.
title: Login status oracle: locked/disabled accounts answer 429 vs 401 by default (account enumeration)

description: mfa.StepUpHandler re-issues the full access+refresh pair after a valid second factor but only propagates Claims.MustChangePassword when the host wires WithMustChangeResolver (mfa/handlers.go:450, nil by default). The interim token minted by identity.LoginHandler's MFA gate DOES carry the flag, so a must-change, MFA-enrolled user who completes step-up on default wiring receives a fresh refresh family with flag=false; Rotate then replays false on every silent refresh and WithPasswordChangeGate stops diverting. With the default MaxRefreshLifetime=0 (unbounded family lifetime) the evasion persists indefinitely; only the next interactive login re-flags (LoginHandler re-checks PasswordChangeRequired). PoC completes a real recovery-code step-up behind ContextMiddleware and shows the stepped-up JWT lost the flag, while the resolver-wired variant preserves it.
remediation: Preserve by default instead of opt-in: in mfa.StepUpHandler, default the must-change decision to the interim token's verified claims (tokens.ClaimsFromContext[C](r.Context())) when mustChangeResolve is nil, i.e. treat a flagged interim as flagged unless explicitly overridden. Concrete change: mfa/handlers.go StepUpHandler — `if cfg.mustChangeResolve != nil ? cfg.mustChangeResolve(r) : interimMustChangeFromContext(r)` where the fallback reads ClaimsFromContext[C]. Keep WithMustChangeResolver as an override, and document that custom StepUpClaimsBuilders must re-check identity.PasswordChangeRequired.
title: MFA step-up drops MustChangePassword by default (forced-password-change bypass)

description: identity.RequestMagicLink and identity.RequestPasswordReset mint single-use tokens for administratively DISABLED accounts (memory and pgx CreateVerificationToken gate only on DeletedAt, never DisabledAt) and return them to the caller for delivery, while unknown identifiers yield ("", nil, nil). The shipped handlers mask this with a uniform 204, but Service-API consumers that branch on the token/user return (or on mailer invocation) get a liveness signal, and suspended users keep receiving credential emails. The consume-time gate (consumeForLiveUser rejects DisabledAt) only fires later, after delivery. PoC shows non-empty tokens minted for a disabled account vs empty for unknown, and that the reset token is still correctly rejected at consume time.
remediation: Enforce the disabled check at mint time, mirroring consumeForLiveUser: in RequestMagicLink/RequestPasswordReset/RequestPasswordResetViaRecovery (and RequestEmailVerification), return ("", nil, nil) after a decoyToken() when the resolved user has DisabledAt set. Concrete change: identity/service.go — after FindUserByEmail success, `if user.DisabledAt != nil { s.decoyToken(); return "", nil, nil }`. Optionally extend the pgx/memory CreateVerificationToken EXISTS guards with `AND disabled_at IS NULL` as defense-in-depth.
title: Password-reset / magic-link tokens minted for disabled accounts (issuance-time liveness gap)

description: The OAuth state cookie (default name "oauth_state", no __Host- prefix) carries the CSRF state + PKCE verifier + nonce + provider + tenant with HMAC integrity ONLY when the host sets WithStateSigningKey; otherwise packState/unpackState accept any well-formed 5-field value (oauth/state.go, oauth/handlers.go). An attacker able to plant cookies (sibling-subdomain tossing — the auth cookies are __Host- protected but the state cookie is not) can forge a state cookie without a Begin round trip and pair it with their own authorization-response link, driving the victim's browser through CallbackHandler into a session bound to the attacker's linked identity (login CSRF). State-cookie HMAC signing alone would not stop a Begin-capable attacker either; the missing control is browser-key binding (e.g. __Host- prefix). PoC proves unsigned forged cookies verify and signed mode rejects them.
remediation: Harden the state cookie by default: (1) default the state cookie name to a __Host- prefixed value and validate Secure/no-Domain/Path=/ like tokens.Cookies.Validate does; (2) warn (or fail) when WithStateSigningKey is unset in non-test builds — concrete change: oauth/handlers.go newHandlerConfig + a startup Validate() on handlerConfig mirroring tokens.Cookies.Validate. Document that cross-subdomain deployments needing a shared state cookie must explicitly opt out and accept the login-CSRF residual.
title: OAuth state cookie unsigned and not host-locked by default (login-CSRF craftability)
